content:
The [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Mode — the most common value (or values) in a list. Enter your numbers (separated by commas, spaces or new lines) and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Find the mode of a list of numbers — the value that appears most often. A list can have one mode, several modes tied for first place, or no mode at all when every value appears exactly once. The mode is the only average that works for categories as well as numbers: the most common shoe size, the most frequent survey answer, or the most repeated test score are all modes. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Mode Calculator

Start by typing or pasting your numbers (separated by commas, spaces or new lines). The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause. The steps below walk through each input in order.

1. Paste or type your numbers, separated by commas, spaces or new lines.
2. Read the mode and how many times it appears.
3. If several values tie, they are all listed.

## Formula

Count how many times each value appears. The mode is the value with the highest count. If two values tie for the highest count, the list is bimodal; if every value appears once, there is no mode.

That is the standard formula for this calculation, and it is the same one the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) applies to the values you enter. You can work it out by hand, but the calculator is faster when you want to try several values, and it removes the risk of a slip in the arithmetic.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. The mode of 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7 and 9 is 7: it appears 3 times, more than any other value. Try the same figures in the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Numbers (separated by commas, spaces or new lines): 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9), the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) returns Mode: 7, Times it appears: 3, Count: 7, Distinct values: 4. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Percentage Calculator](/percentage-calculator) is worth a look before you finish.

## One mode, two modes, no mode

A list with a clear winner is unimodal; a list where two values tie for the top count is bimodal, and both are reported. When every value appears exactly once there is no mode — nothing is more common than anything else. A list like 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 has two modes (1 and 2), each appearing twice.

## Mode for categories, not just numbers

Mean and median need numbers, but the mode works for anything you can count: the most common eye colour in a class, the most popular pizza topping, or the most frequent error in a log file. That is why the mode is the standard “average” for survey answers and other categorical data.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- The mode is the most common value — count, don't sort.
- A tie means more than one mode; the calculator lists them all.
- For survey answers and categories, the mode is the only average that applies.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the mode?

The value that appears most often in a list of numbers. For 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 7, 9 the mode is 7, which appears 3 times. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Can a list have more than one mode?

Yes. If two values tie for the highest count, both are modes — the list is bimodal. The calculator lists every tied value. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What if every number appears only once?

Then there is no mode. Nothing is more common than anything else, so the calculator says so instead of picking a value at random. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the mode used for?

Finding the most common value: the most frequent test score, the most common shoe size, or the most popular answer in a survey. Try it with your own numbers in the [Mode Calculator](/mode-calculator) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.
